# Implement block: Photo Vortex Morph (SwiftUI)

You are adding the "Photo Vortex Morph" block from Native Cook to the user's iOS app. The block already exists as working SwiftUI code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

Forty small photos (fashion editorials, film stills, gallery rooms and interiors) on an off-white sheet that morph between five layouts, every card travelling on its own spring a beat after its neighbour and tumbling a little on the way. They open as a vortex: a ring of overlapping portrait cards, each turned past its spoke like the petals of a flower around a small hole, turning slowly. Then they burst into a drift of little cards floating in depth, near ones larger, the whole field turning slowly; gather into a single neat stack in the middle; fan into a horizontal strip of thin slivers with the last card open in full; and settle into a five-by-eight grid laid edge to edge over the whole screen. Small tracked capitals at the top read "Kinetic Archive" and the layout's number, "01 / 05"; the layout's name and a line about it sit at the bottom left with "Tap to morph" at the right, all set in white with a difference blend so they read dark on paper and light on photos.

**Motion.** All forty cards are drawn on one canvas, each through its own perspective transform. Each card is a damped spring per property (centre, size, turn in the plane, tip about both axes, and drawing order), stiffness 150 times a per-card factor between 0.8 and 1.2 and damping ratio 0.74, integrated in 1/120 s steps every frame. On a change each card waits its turn so the move runs as a wave (vortex: up to 0.32 s by index; drift: up to 0.45 s; stack: by distance from the middle, up to 0.3 s, lower cards on softer springs; strip: from the last card back, up to 0.28 s; grid: diagonally, 0.032 s per cell), and as it leaves it is kicked into a spin of 2.6 rad/s and a tip of 1.6 rad/s, a different way per card, so it tumbles before settling. Vortex: cards 27% of the width wide at 3:4, on a ring 25% of the width in radius, each turned 0.5 rad past tangent; the ring turns once per 14.4 s, opens by up to 16% of its radius when spun fast, and once settled is drawn twice with its overlap seam on opposite sides so no card visibly ends the ring. Drift: cards 13.5% of the width scattered on a jittered 5 by 8 grid through a box 70% by 42% of the screen and 70% of the width deep, seen from 1.6 widths away, each tipped by up to 0.55 rad, bobbing 5 pt three times per loop, the box turning at 0.11 rad/s. Stack: 42% by 56% of the width, cards under the top one off by up to 4 pt and 0.05 rad. Strip: cards 34% by 45% of the width overlapping so each shows a 1.2% sliver, the open one in full. Grid: 5 by 8 over the whole screen, 2 pt gaps. Tap moves on to the next layout with a light haptic; the caption crosses over in 0.45 s, the new one rising 10 pt. Dragging spins the vortex with the finger about the middle and a flick keeps it spinning (up to 14 rad/s, the extra fading at 1.4 per second); drag turns the drift (0.005 rad per pt) and tips it (0.0035 rad per pt, up to 0.45 rad), the tip springing back on release (650 ms, damping ratio 0.62) and the turn carrying the flick's speed; drag slides the strip open one card per 9 pt, rubber-banding past either end and landing on the card the throw was heading for with a selection haptic (520 ms, damping ratio 0.9); drag pulls the stack or the grid with resistance (up to 140 pt) and it springs back with the finger's speed. autoPlay: LOOP 14.4 s from a settled, turning vortex; drift at 2.4 s, stack at 5.0 s, strip at 7.0 s (sliding open card 28 at 7.9 s and back at 8.6 s), grid at 9.4 s and back to the vortex at 11.8 s, settled again before the loop restarts. A touch pauses it for 3 s, after which it picks up from the current layout. Photos fade in over 0.35 s as they load. Under reduced motion autoPlay is off, nothing turns or tumbles, and a tap fades the cards out in 160 ms, jumps to the next layout and fades back in over 220 ms.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [PhotoVortexMorphDemo.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Media/PhotoVortexMorph/PhotoVortexMorphDemo.swift)

### Files of the block

- [PhotoVortexMorph.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Media/PhotoVortexMorph/PhotoVortexMorph.swift)
- [PhotoVortexMorphEngine.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Media/PhotoVortexMorph/PhotoVortexMorphEngine.swift)

### Used by the demo only

- [swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift)

### Frameworks

It needs no framework beyond SwiftUI.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced iOS engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference in the iOS Simulator or on a device. A SwiftUI preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and curves. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an iOS app built with Xcode (an `.xcodeproj`, an `.xcworkspace` or a Swift package with an app target). If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app target, its deployment target and its Swift version.
- SwiftUI, UIKit or both, and how a screen is shown today: `NavigationStack`, a coordinator, a tab bar, a storyboard.
- How files join the target: a folder the project synchronises, or a file list in the project that you have to extend.
- Conventions: folder layout, naming, where colours, fonts and assets live.
- Type names the app already uses, so the block's types do not collide with them.

### 3. Read the block

- Swift files in a module do not import each other, so the demo alone will not lead you to the rest. The list above names every file of the block: read them all.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's initialiser and its defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- The source app targets iOS 17. If the host targets an older system, check each API the block uses and tell the user what would have to change before you lower anything. Do not raise the host's deployment target without asking.
- If a type or function name of the block already exists in the app, rename the block's one, in every file that uses it, and say that you did.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block uses next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.
- In a UIKit app, show the block through a `UIHostingController`.

### 5. Bring it in

- Add the block's files to the app target, keeping their names.
- Copy its asset catalogs, loose resources and fonts, and check that the names the code asks for match the names in the bundle: a wrong name compiles and then shows nothing.
- A `.metal` file has to be compiled into the same target as the code that calls its function.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build the app target for a simulator with `xcodebuild` or the project's own script, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Run it and use the block: every state, every gesture, light and dark appearance if the block follows them, and once with Reduce Motion on.
- If the build or the simulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
